response_text:
## Plain-language version

**Figure 4 data: Perinatal deaths by state, 2022 vs. 2023**

The perinatal mortality rate counts babies who die shortly before or shortly after birth. It's expressed as deaths per 1,000 births — so a rate of 9.44 means about 9 such deaths for every 1,000 births.

This table shows the rate for each state in 2022 and again in 2023, and whether the change between those two years was large enough to be a real shift rather than ordinary year-to-year fluctuation. A dagger (†) marks changes that were **not** statistically meaningful — the numbers moved, but not by enough to conclude anything changed. Where a percentage appears instead, the change was real.

For the states shown in this excerpt:

| State | 2022 | 2023 | What changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alabama | 9.44 | 10.96 | Rose 16% — a real increase |
| Alaska | 8.39 | 7.73 | Drop not meaningful |
| Arizona | 9.56 | 9.28 | Drop not meaningful |
| Arkansas | 10.86 | 11.49 | Rise not meaningful |
| California | 7.30 | 7.25 | Essentially unchanged |
| Colorado | 7.32 | 8.61 | Rose 18% — a real increase |
| Connecticut | 6.93 | 7.63 | Rise not meaningful |
| Delaware | 9.66 | 8.68 | Drop not meaningful |

**The takeaway:** Among these states, only Alabama and Colorado saw increases big enough to count as genuine change — up 16% and 18%, respectively. Everywhere else, the year-to-year movement falls within normal statistical noise. Rates in this group ranged from under 7 per 1,000 (Connecticut, California) to over 11 (Arkansas).

Two notes on the source: the full figure covers all 50 states and the District of Columbia, but the text you provided stops at Delaware — so this is an alphabetical excerpt, not the complete picture. And "statistically significant" here uses the standard p = 0.05 threshold, meaning a change is only flagged as real if there's less than a 1-in-20 chance it's a fluke.
